forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Up 1pp to 28% (CI [15,42] from [14,41]). The single material development is that the Erdos unit-distance result priced yesterday at roughly +1 turned out to be the leading edge of a much larger release: OpenAI's 1 August paper 'Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science' attributes solutions to TEN open problems, each unsolved for a decade or more, to an internal version of Astra, explicitly teased as its 'next major model'. The full scope only propagated through press in the 2-4 August window (TechTimes 2 Aug, Forbes and Quartz 3 Aug, The Decoder, BleepingComputer, DataCamp), so most of it postdates yesterday's evidence base. Details that matter for resolution: a 249-page manuscript with Lean 4 proof certificates on GitHub (zero 'sorry' placeholders, i.e. fully machine-verified), results including a non-sofic groups construction (a central open question in group theory) and new closest-vector-problem bounds relevant to lattice cryptography, total token cost ~$2,000 at Sol API rates; Thomas Bloom (erdosproblems.com) called the constructions 'big news' and bigger than the unit-distance counterexample, and OpenAI's Sebastien Bubeck confirmed each result ships with a Lean certificate. This is exactly the 'multiple independently-verified novel research results' condition in yesterday's update triggers, partially met within one release from one lab - hence a disciplined +1 rather than more. Capping the move: commentators uniformly frame it as a powerful specialized tool rather than AGI (ETCJournal 1 Aug and others), the Leiden Declaration backdrop shows the mathematics community policing AI claims hard, no researcher made an AGI-achieved statement in the 4-5 Aug window, the ARC-AGI-3 harness dispute remains unadjudicated (official leaderboard still Opus 5 at 30.2%, Sol's 38.3% self-reported and unverified on the private set), and Pacing the Frontier's institutional endorsements by OpenAI and Anthropic keep the anti-declaration norm intact. Nothing new on EO 14409: the 1 Aug deadline lapsed with zero published deliverables (Neomanex, Vorp Labs), consistent with what was already priced.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: expert and market forecasts for announcement-based AGI within ~3.4 years. Prediction markets in late July 2026 put ~10% on OpenAI achieving AGI by 2027; Metaculus-style aggregates for weak/announced AGI cluster medians in the early-to-mid 2030s, implying roughly 20-30% probability mass before 2030; AAAI 2025 survey found 76% of AI researchers doubt pure scaling reaches AGI. Historical base rate of confidently predicted transformative-tech milestones arriving on schedule is low (fusion, full self-driving), arguing against the high end. The announcement-based resolution criterion sits above pure-capability base rates because commercial and contractual incentives to declare exist, but below hype-implied rates because the 3+ leading-researcher bar is policed hard.

factors_up.factor: Astra 'Ten advances' release: ten decade-plus open problems solved with fully machine-verified Lean proofs for ~$2,000 of compute, including non-sofic groups and CVP bounds; Bloom calls it 'big news', Gowers previously said Annals-worthy - first sustained crossing from benchmarks into verifiable original research
Astra explicitly framed as OpenAI's 'next major model' - a flagship materially stronger than Sol is now confirmed in-house, compressing expected capability timelines
EO 14409 framework deadline lapsed 1 Aug with zero deliverables; regulatory vacuum official, no enacted brake on the frontier
Large inference-time headroom demonstrated by retained-reasoning/compaction settings (Sol 7.8% to 38.3% on ARC-AGI-3), even if leaderboard-disputed

factors_down.factor: Uniform expert framing of Astra results as specialized tool, not general intelligence; Leiden Declaration shows mathematics community actively gatekeeping AI claims
Pacing the Frontier institutionally endorsed by OpenAI and Anthropic plus 1,100+ lab employees including chief scientists - formalized norm against racing to and declaring AGI
3+ leading-researcher resolution bar policed hard; no AGI-achieved statements from any credible researcher despite the Astra release

ARC-AGI-3 official SOTA still only 30.2% (Opus 5); Sol's higher figure unverified, and government showed willingness to suspend frontier models (Fable 5/Mythos 5 June suspension) - interventionist tail risk

key_uncertainties: Whether Astra's public release (timing unknown) shows generality gains matching its mathematics performance, or the math results prove narrow
Whether AI-originated research results cascade into elite-researcher statements that AGI-level capability has arrived, or the Leiden-style gatekeeping hardens
Whether the lapsed EO 14409 framework re-emerges as de facto mandatory pre-release review, given June-July showed the government will suspend models ad hoc
Whether the ARC Prize adjudicates retained-reasoning settings as legitimate, and whether scaffolding gains generalize to open-ended autonomy
Whether the announcement-based resolution bar drifts as commercial incentives to declare AGI grow (IPO-era labs)
update_triggers: Revise UP if Astra launches publicly with frontier-generality results (e.g. >60% ARC-AGI-3 official) or is framed by OpenAI as 'AGI-class'
Revise UP if independent mathematicians or other labs replicate/extend AI-originated open-problem results and leading researchers begin framing this as AGI-level
Revise UP if the EO 14409 framework is formally abandoned and no successor process emerges
Revise DOWN if a published EO 14409 framework establishes functioning pre-release review with broad lab compliance
Revise DOWN if Pacing the Frontier converts into binding international pacing mechanisms
Revise DOWN if Astra's public release disappoints on generality benchmarks, indicating the math results were narrow-domain

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 22% (CI [11,36]). Searches on 4-5 August surfaced no new trigger-level events, only continued churn of the known storylines. The McKinsey cuts story (up to ~10% of non-client-facing staff, ~200 internal tech/support roles already automated away, with commentary pieces in Fast Company/Inc and Quartz framing it as an AI warning signal for consulting) remains the dominant narrative but was already fully priced in yesterday. Aggregators this week confirm the running tally unchanged: KPMG ~400 US advisory cuts, Accenture cutting staff who cannot be retrained for AI-era delivery while simultaneously spending $4.1bn to acquire cybersecurity AI firm Dragos, and Bain/BCG/Deloitte slowing hiring. One incrementally useful datapoint: UK Big Four graduate intakes cut 6-30% (Deloitte ~-18%, EY -11%, PwC -6%), explicitly tied to AI replacing rookie tasks - this corroborates the Revelio Labs pyramid-compression signal already in yesterday's forecast rather than adding new information. Countervailing evidence also unchanged and firm: EY reported AI-related revenues up 30% in FY2025, MCA/PRNewswire January release shows UK consultants forecasting higher growth in 2026 on surging digital/AI demand, and Avasant characterises 2026 as 'growth normalization' with revenue convergence, not contraction. The pattern remains junior/back-office compression plus top-line resilience from selling AI services - exactly the audit/legal-discovery template that never reached -33%. No daily move warranted.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: major professional-services sectors hit by prior automation waves (audit post-digitisation, legal discovery post-e-discovery, IT services post-offshoring). None lost ≥33% of revenue or employment within six years of the technology shock; the typical pattern is 10-20% junior-role pyramid compression alongside top-line growth from selling the disruptive technology as a service. Base rate for a ≥33% sector-wide contraction attributed primarily to a single technology within ~6 years: well under 15%; consulting's current AI-revenue offset argues for the low end.

factors_up.factor: AI-linked headcount rationalisation continuing at scale: McKinsey up to ~10% of non-client-facing staff, Accenture retrain-or-exit policy, KPMG ~400 US advisory cuts, Bain/BCG/Deloitte hiring slowdowns
Structural pyramid compression at intake: UK Big Four graduate intakes cut 6-30% on AI grounds; Revelio Labs shows consulting hiring demand ~20% below 2023 peak
Deloitte scrapping analyst-consultant-manager titles for ~181,500 US staff from June 2026, explicitly framed around AI reshaping the pyramid

factors_down.factor: Revenue offset from selling AI: EY AI revenues +30% FY2025; Source Global Research sees tech consulting passing $400bn (+7%) in 2026; MCA projects UK sector growth 5.7% (2026) and 7.4% (2027)
Historical precedent: no comparable professional-services sector has contracted ≥33% within six years of an automation shock
Resolution requires ≥33% decline PLUS primary AI attribution by 2+ credible analyses - cuts so far are attributed to mixed causes (soft demand, restructuring, AI)

key_uncertainties: Whether AI agents move from back-office automation to displacing core client-facing advisory revenue by 2028-29
Whether firms' AI-services revenue growth continues to offset headcount compression in top-line terms
How 'consultancy revenue or employment' is measured at resolution (sector-wide vs firm-level, and which analyses count as credible attribution)
update_triggers: Revise UP if a Big 4 or MBB firm reports an annual revenue decline >10% explicitly attributed to AI substitution, or announces client-facing (not back-office) cuts >15% of consulting headcount
Revise UP if sector-wide consulting employment data (BLS/ONS or Source Global Research) shows cumulative decline >10% from 2024 baseline
Revise DOWN if 2026 full-year sector revenue growth comes in at or above the projected 5-7% with stable total employment

forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: post-war UK governing parties seeking re-election retained most seats in roughly 11 of 20 contests (~55%), but polling 3+ years out has weak predictive power (Major 1990-92 and Blair mid-terms saw >10pp swings). In a fragmented three-way race under FPTP (Lab/Ref/Con all at 19-27%), seat outcomes are hypersensitive to small vote shifts, arguing for probabilities near 40-55% for the current polling leader. Sources: House of Commons Library CBP-8647; PollCheck/BritPolls aggregates.

This is exactly the whipsaw pattern flagged yesterday, and it remains far from the pre-registered trigger (Brent below $70 and holding 3+ weeks before end-September). Every structural anchor was reconfirmed by today's searches: Cornwall Insight still forecasts the October Ofgem cap at ~GBP 1,899/yr, a further ~2% rise on July's GBP 1,862, with the final level to be published by 26 August; the House of Commons Library update confirms independent forecasters surveyed by HM Treasury expect CPI around 3.5% in Q4 2026; NIESR's late-July forecast has inflation exceeding the 2% target until 2029 with 2026 averaging 3.1%; and there is no August MPC meeting - the 30 July decision (hold at 3.75%, with Greene, Mann and Pill voting to hike) stands, and the next decision is 17 September. With June CPI at 2.6%, a projected rising path to ~3.2% in Q4, and only the July-November prints able to resolve YES, sub-2.0% remains outside every published forecast range. Nothing dated 4-5 Aug changes that; hold.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: months where UK CPI printed below 2.0% when the starting rate was 2.5%+ with a central-bank-projected rising path five months from the deadline - essentially unprecedented absent a demand collapse. CPI has printed below 2.0% in only one month since mid-2021 (Sep 2024, 1.7%). A 0.7pp+ fall against a projected ~0.6pp rise within five publishable prints has no post-1997 precedent outside the 2008 and 2014-15 oil crashes, both involving 50%+ oil price declines; the current situation is a partially-retraced upward oil shock (Brent ~$85 on 4 Aug vs ~$126 April peak). Sources: ONS CPI series D7G7, BoE July 2026 MPR.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 34% (CI unchanged [21,48]). The 4-5 August window contained no structural news for a 2030s-horizon question. Gilt markets were quiet: the 10-year yield rose 4bp to 4.99% on 4 Aug (TradingEconomics), essentially flat around the 5% level priced since end-July, with the market narrative unchanged - Healey's adherence-to-fiscal-rules line has steadied gilts and sterling, and clarity awaits the autumn Budget. Two secondary datapoints surfaced, roughly offsetting. Mildly positive: fresh circulation of the Bennett School/ONS-adjacent analysis that alternative RTI-based measures show labour productivity up ~5.5% since 2019 versus ~2.5% on the LFS-based series - if productivity is being under-measured, the true starting trend entering the 2030s is somewhat better than official statistics imply, though resolution depends on ONS-reported GDP, so mismeasurement cuts both ways. Mildly negative: renewed attention to the OBR's central estimate that AI adds only ~0.2pp to annual productivity growth by the forecast horizon (Briefing Paper No.9 lineage), well short of the ~0.5pp+ acceleration the 1.5% bar effectively requires, and its downside scenario of 0.3% trend productivity. NIESR's late-July round (2026 growth upgraded 0.9% to 1.1%, inflation above target until 2029) was already reflected in the Treasury-survey anchor priced yesterday. No new OBR, BoE or OECD long-run publications, no Budget signal, no measured productivity inflection. All structural anchors (OBR potential at/below 1.5%, BoE ~1.4%, OECD ~1%) stand; hold.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: UK decade-average real GDP growth - 2.9% (1980s), 2.1% (1990s), 1.8% (2000s incl. GFC), 2.0% (2010s), and an estimated ~1.3-1.5% for the 2020s to date; post-2008 trend growth has sat near 1-1.5% for 15+ years. Institutional long-run projections cluster below the bar: OBR trend at or below ~1.5% after the March 2026 productivity downgrade, BoE potential ~1.4%, OECD long-term ~1%, and the Treasury's July survey of independent forecasters averages ~1.0% growth for 2026 and 2027 (NIESR 1.1% for 2026). Exceeding 1.5% for a full decade average therefore requires a productivity regime change (e.g. AI diffusion) or sustained above-trend catch-up. Sources: ONS ABMI series, OBR EFO March 2026, OECD long-term scenarios.

factors_up.factor: BoE scenarios converge to 1.6-1.7% annual growth by 2028-29, giving positive momentum into the decade
Potential AI/technology-driven productivity acceleration not embedded in official trend estimates, with active government adoption push (G7-fastest-adopter pledge, AI economics institute)
Alternative RTI-based productivity measures suggest ~5.5% growth since 2019 vs ~2.5% on LFS-based series - underlying trend may be stronger than official data imply
Post-energy-shock normalisation plus possible catch-up growth early in the 2030s

factors_down.factor: Official potential-growth estimates (BoE ~1.4%, OECD ~1%, OBR downgraded again in March 2026) all at or below the 1.5% bar; OBR's central AI uplift is only ~0.2pp/yr
G7-highest gilt yields (10yr ~5.0% on 4 Aug), oil-driven inflation risk and priced BoE hikes suppress 2020s investment and the capital stock entering the 2030s
Demographics: shrinking workforce growth, lower net migration assumptions, and rising old-age dependency through the 2030s

key_uncertainties: Whether AI adoption produces a measurable UK productivity acceleration by the early 2030s, beyond survey-reported firm-level gains and the OBR's ~0.2pp central estimate
Whether the Healey Treasury's autumn Budget maintains the inherited fiscal rules and the resulting gilt-market path
Long-run energy costs given the Middle East conflict's oil-price shock and the Hormuz diplomacy
Migration policy and labour-supply growth through the 2030s
Whether ONS measurement (LFS vs RTI productivity divergence) and revisions shift the decade mean around the 1.5% threshold
update_triggers: Revise UP if OBR or BoE upgrade UK potential/trend growth to 1.5%+ in a future forecast round
Revise UP if UK productivity growth sustains 1.5%+ annualised for 4+ consecutive quarters
Revise UP if gilt yields fall materially (10-year below 4%) easing the investment constraint
Revise DOWN if the autumn Budget abandons fiscal rules and triggers a sustained gilt selloff (10-year above 5.5%)
Revise DOWN if the 2020s decade average finishes below 1.2%, indicating entrenched sub-trend momentum
Revise DOWN if measured AI productivity effects disappoint in US/UK data through 2027-28
